summary: A statement from the IAB and IESG about cryptographic technology, saying that privacy and protection of commercial transactions require wide availability of strong cryptography. It is a best current practice document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1984 is a 1996 statement from the bodies that oversee Internet architecture and standards. It says that privacy and safe online commerce depend on strong encryption, and that policies restricting encryption hurt users and businesses while giving little benefit. It is an Informational memo, not a protocol.

subtitle: The IAB and IESG argue against export controls, weak keys and key escrow for cryptography.

tldr.problem: Governments had actual or proposed policies that restrict cryptography, which the IAB and IESG saw as harming privacy, commerce and trust on the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: The statement lists four kinds of restrictive policy, then gives a technical analysis covering key size, certification authorities, key escrow, signature keys, data recovery and conflicting national rules.
tldr.outcome: It concludes that cryptography is the most powerful single tool for securing the Internet, and that knowingly making it weaker has no proven benefit.

facts.label: Policy types opposed
facts.value: 4 (export controls, weak keys, mandated key holding, prohibition)

today: RFC 1984 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It states a position rather than defining a protocol.

sections.title: The Concern
sections.content:
The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) and the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG), the bodies that oversee Internet architecture and standards, state their concern for stronger protection of international commercial transactions and for adequate privacy for all Internet users. The security mechanisms being developed in the IETF depend on the international use of adequate cryptographic technology, so ready access to that technology is a key factor in the Internet's growth.

They are disturbed by government policies that impose export controls, restrict commercial and private users to weak mechanisms such as short keys, mandate that private decryption keys be held by the government or another third party, or prohibit cryptology entirely or permit it only to specially authorized organizations. They encourage policies that allow ready access to uniform strong cryptography for all Internet users in all countries.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet's oversight bodies worry that some governments limit who may use strong encryption and how strong it may be. They want strong encryption freely available to everyone.

sections.title: The Claims
sections.content:
The statement claims that the Internet is becoming the predominant vehicle for electronic commerce and information exchange, and that its support structure must be trustworthy. Encryption is not a secret technology monopolized by one country: any hobbyist can program a PC to do powerful encryption, and many algorithms are well documented, some with source code available in textbooks.

Export controls place companies in the controlling country at a competitive disadvantage, because competitors elsewhere can sell systems whose only design constraint is being secure and easy to use. Usage controls do the same by blocking secure electronic commerce. Escrow mechanisms inevitably weaken the security of the overall cryptographic system by creating new points of vulnerability that can and will be attacked. Meanwhile the controls slow the deployment of security just as the Internet is growing exponentially and attackers are becoming more sophisticated.
sections.plainLanguage: Strong encryption is widely known, so blocking it mostly penalizes honest companies. Storing spare copies of private keys adds new weak points that attackers can target.

sections.title: Technical Analysis
sections.content:
The analysis has several parts. On key size, restricting use or export by key size is not acceptable: systems breakable by one country are breakable by others, large organizations and criminal enterprises have the resources to break many systems, and conversations often need protection for years, so as computers speed up, key sizes once out of reach of cryptanalysis become insecure.

On public key infrastructure, certification authorities are legitimate and necessary, and many governments will and should run their own, but they must not be confused with escrow centers: certification authorities deal with public keys, while escrow centers store private keys, and sound practice says users never reveal their private keys to anyone, even the certification authority. Since a modern cryptosystem's security rests entirely on the secrecy of the keys, secret keys should never leave the user's secure environment, and escrow contradicts that. Data recovery should be the customer's choice. Keys used for signatures and authentication must never be escrowed, because a third party with access could impersonate the legitimate owner and non-repudiation, one of the most important uses for cryptography, depends on only the user having the private key.

The analysis also notes that conventional passwords and credit card numbers must be protected by strong encryption, that conflicting national restrictions force international companies to use weak encryption, that escrow does not stop someone from using another encryption scheme first, and that perfect forward secrecy is generally incompatible with escrow of private keys, which the RFC calls an oversimplification of a longer analysis.
sections.plainLanguage: The technical case says weak or government-held keys fail in practice: keys become breakable over time, signature keys could be misused to impersonate their owners, and only the user should hold a private key.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content: The statement concludes that as more companies connect and more commerce happens online, security becomes more critical. Cryptography is the most powerful single tool users can use to secure the Internet, and knowingly making it weaker threatens their ability to do so and has no proven benefit. The Security Considerations section says security issues are discussed throughout the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: Its conclusion is short: strong encryption is the best tool available for online safety, and weakening it does not clearly help anyone.
